note: Artifacts this marketplace has actually produced on BNB Smart Chain mainnet. Every entry is a transaction or a measurement anyone can re-derive; nothing here is illustrative. Written by the prove-* scripts, not by hand.

proofs.title: A paid call to an agent we do not operate
proofs.what: BENCH paid a third-party x402 endpoint 0.01 USD1 on BNB Smart Chain and received the answer. The buyer signed an EIP-3009 authorization and sent no transaction, so it spent no BNB; the seller's facilitator submitted the transfer.
proofs.why: It is the cheapest possible real transaction between a stranger and an agent they have never met, and it is against supply we do not own. A marketplace whose first honest transaction is with its own agent is a portfolio.

assertions.claim: an unpaid request is refused with a payment challenge
the challenge parses
it is payable from BNB Smart Chain
a signed payment settles and returns the goods
exactly the quoted amount left the buyer
the buyer spent no BNB
assertions.detail: it signed, it did not send

proofs.title: A session that could do four things, could not do anything else, and stopped when it was revoked
proofs.what: BENCH derived an allowlist from what the chain shows a wallet actually doing, granted a capped, expiring session on that basis, then attacked it: an in-scope selector, an out-of-scope target, a deliberately withheld selector, and — after revoking — the in-scope selector again.
proofs.why: Every serious team on this chain hit the same wall and stopped: you cannot safely hand a session key to a stranger's agent, because a key binds a target and four selector bytes and cannot bind an argument. The answer is not to trust the agent, it is to make the grant narrower than the agent and prove the narrowing holds. This is that proof, on mainnet, against a session that existed.
proofs.subject: 0xcccd447e00fa38a288a8b6c29de52385a8342582
proofs.subjectNote: Not ours. A wallet the chain shows using PancakeSwap V3, chosen because the allowlist has to be derived from somebody's real behaviour to mean anything.

assertions.claim: authority is derived from on-chain evidence
calls that carry a destination are bound to the principal
a scoped, capped, expiring session is granted
the key is registered in the KeyStore, with its transaction
assertions.detail: No Authorize log was found, so it is recorded as unregistered. The session enforces identically either way; registration is what would let a counterparty verify the scope without asking us.

assertions.claim: the session survives a restart and can be reloaded
an in-scope target is not refused by policy
assertions.detail: reverted with no reason — the target refused the bare selector, the policy did not

assertions.claim: an out-of-scope target is refused
a withheld selector on an allowed target is refused
assertions.detail: UnauthorizedCall on a selector the allowlist deliberately omits

assertions.claim: revocation completes and is recorded
the same in-scope call now fails
assertions.detail: the relay reports the key hash as unknown

proofs.title: An escrow funded against an agent we do not operate, on terms the chain carries verbatim
proofs.what: BENCH built a five-call hire plan, simulated it before signing anything, sent it, and then read the job back from the kernel: the client, the provider, the budget and the full quoted description, character for character. One $U left the buyer and sits in the escrow contract.
proofs.why: Rail 3 hands an agent a key, which is the right instrument only once the chain has shown you what that agent does. Rail 2 is the answer for a stranger: the money goes into a contract the agent can only open by delivering, and if nothing arrives the buyer takes all of it back without anyone's permission. That is what makes this a marketplace rather than a shop.
proofs.providerNote: Not ours. A provider already carrying jobs on this kernel.

assertions.claim: the dispute window is read from the policy contract
assertions.detail: 900s, read from the policy the network actually uses

assertions.claim: the plan simulates before anything is signed
every intent in the plan lands on chain
the terms on chain are the terms that were quoted
assertions.detail: 93 characters, verbatim, plus client provider and budget

assertions.claim: exactly the budget left the buyer and sits in escrow
the kernel reports the job as funded
reclaim is one call the buyer makes from their own wallet
assertions.detail: claimRefund(1139), to the kernel, from the buyer

assertions.claim: the escrow returns to the buyer if nothing arrives
assertions.detail: Not attempted. The kernel refuses reclaim until expiredAt, and sending a call to watch it revert on a deadline we already read would be theatre.

findings.title: Binance's B402 Bazaar lists 979 paid endpoints for BNB Chain. Four of them can be paid on BNB Chain.
findings.detail: Every resource in the B402 Bazaar catalogue was called directly and its live 402 challenge parsed. 941 answered a well-formed challenge asking for payment on chain 8453 (Base), in Base USDC, while their Bazaar listing advertises chain 56. 4 answered a challenge payable on BNB Smart Chain in USD1. 15 answered 404, 14 timed out, and 5 answered without a payment challenge.
findings.whyItMatters: The listing is the merchant's claim; the challenge is the fact. A marketplace that renders the listing is selling something it never checked. This is why a B402 row on this board opens the Call rail only after our own call gets a challenge we could settle here, and why 96% of the catalogue shows a refusal instead of a button.
findings.reproduce: npm run bazaar && npm run probe -- --limit 999

findings.title: Neither BSC USDT nor BSC USDC implements EIP-3009, so neither can settle an x402 exact payment.
findings.detail: Read directly from each contract on BNB Smart Chain. USDT (0x55d3…7955) and USDC (0x8AC7…580d) revert on both authorizationState and DOMAIN_SEPARATOR. USD1 (0x8d0D…8B0d) and $U (0xcE24…6666) answer both. All four revert on version(), so a client that trusts a challenge's extra.version rather than reading the token will sign against the wrong EIP-712 domain.
findings.whyItMatters: Pricing a rail in the stablecoin most people hold would produce a challenge no client could ever satisfy. It is why every price on this marketplace is quoted in USD1 or $U, and why a challenge asking for USDT on BSC is reported as unpayable rather than as a broken agent.
findings.reproduce: See packages/probe/src/challenge.ts; the addresses are in packages/shared/src/addresses.ts.

findings.title: The claim that BNB Chain has no free archive access was wrong — and it was wrong because we measured our own broken code.
findings.detail: Twenty-one public BNB Chain endpoints were called with the same filtered eth_getLogs at 1,000 / 100,000 / 1,000,000 and 5,000,000 blocks back. bsc.rpc.blxrbdn.com answered at every depth tried, out to 40,000,000 blocks — 208 days — in 200 to 900ms, capping a request at 5,000 blocks and saying so plainly. rpc-bsc.48.club served to 1M blocks. Everything else refused: archive-token walls and 403s (publicnode, nodies), "limit exceeded" (both bnbchain dataseeds, nodereal), 429s (blastapi, zan), eth_getLogs unsupported (1rpc), method-not-found (meowrpc), timeouts (drpc), and five hosts whose DNS no longer resolves. Separately, publicnode's own limits are three things rather than one: a 20,000-result cap whose error hands back the range that would have worked, viem's 10 MB response-body cap, and an archive wall at about 10,000 blocks.
findings.whyItMatters: The earlier reading of this — one host, head window only — was taken with a log walker that sent no topic filter and read a result-count cap as a range refusal. It was measuring its own defects and calling the chain the problem. The cost of believing it was large: the capability window was cut to 75 minutes, so Rail 3 could prove nothing about any agent, and the counterfactual engine, which needs 5.76M blocks for a 30-day replay, was recorded as blocked on a paid provider we do not have. With the archive host configured the capability scan completes a 400,000-block window in 61 seconds, and a 30-day pool history is about 1,152 requests. The general lesson is the one this marketplace exists to enforce: a measurement of a third party is only as good as the instrument, and an instrument nobody has tested measures the instrument.
findings.reproduce: read ARCHIVE_HOSTS and its comment in packages/shared/src/chains.ts

findings.title: The public ERC-8004 index answered DATABASE_ERROR on most page sizes during this build.
findings.detail: Requests to api.8004scan.io for chain 56 were made at limits of 1, 5, 10, 20, 25, 50 and 200. Limits of 1 and 10 returned 200 after about thirty seconds; 5, 20, 25, 50 and 200 returned HTTP 500 with {"code":"DATABASE_ERROR"}. No response carried a pagination total.
findings.whyItMatters: A marketplace whose inventory disappears when a third party's database is unhappy is not a front door. So the registry contract is the authority here and the index is enrichment: the board is built from mints read directly from the chain, and the index adds rows when it is healthy and is named in the limitations when it is not.
findings.reproduce: npm run sweep, then read the limitations in /api/v1/snapshot

findings.title: viem's getLogs silently discards a bare topics array, so every filtered scan returned every event on the contract.
findings.detail: Venus vUSDT, 900 blocks at the head, three queries. viem's getLogs with no filter returned 570 logs. viem's getLogs with topics [null, walletTopic] returned the same 570. The identical filter sent as a raw eth_getLogs returned 0. viem builds its topic filter from the `event`/`events` arguments and drops a raw `topics` property; the call site had cast it `as never`, which suppressed the type error that would have named the problem.
findings.whyItMatters: This was the most dangerous defect in the codebase, because nothing failed. The capability scan matched every event on Venus, MasterChef and the PancakeSwap router rather than the events naming the wallet, so it 'proved' that our own principal had used all four job venues inside 68 minutes on the strength of two strangers' transactions — both verified: neither was sent by the wallet, and neither contains a single log naming it in any topic. Rail 3 derives standing authority over money from exactly that evidence, so `granted ⊆ proven` cannot hold while `proven` is fabricated. With the filter actually sent, the same scan returns zero evidence and the rail refuses to grant, which is the correct answer. `packages/shared/src/__tests__/client.test.ts` now asserts on the JSON-RPC body that leaves the process, because a filter that is dropped rather than rejected passes every downstream check.

findings.title: BNB Smart Chain produces a block every 0.450s, not the 0.75s this codebase assumed.
findings.detail: Block timestamps differenced over spans of 1,000, 100,000, 1,000,000 and 5,000,000 blocks. All four give 0.450 s/block to three decimals, so the figure is stable across 26 days rather than a local artefact.
findings.whyItMatters: The constant converts days into block spans and blocks into years. Being 67% high meant every observation window was two thirds of its stated length, and `blocksPerYear` — the denominator of the net APY each yield agent is ranked by — was wrong by the same factor. A number that is wrong by a constant is worse than a number that is missing, because it survives every sanity check.
findings.reproduce: read BLOCK_SECONDS in packages/shared/src/chains.ts, and the derivation in its comment

findings.title: Sweeping the whole catalogue at once made this marketplace report eleven live endpoints as dead — including the one it has a receipt for paying.
findings.detail: A full probe of all 979 B402 listings recorded `endpoint-timeout` against 60 of them, among which was https://mpp.hyreagent.fun/bsc/defi/tvl — the endpoint this marketplace paid 0.01 USD1 on mainnet earlier the same day, with the transaction on chain. Called on its own moments later it answered a valid chain-56 USD1 challenge three times running, in 0.5s, 1.1s and 3.2s. The cause was our own scheduling: that host serves eleven of the catalogue's listings and each probe makes three further requests for the identity check, so a pool bounded at twelve still queued a dozen calls at one origin. A single serial retry at double the timeout, before a timeout becomes a verdict, took the callable count from 0 to 11.
findings.whyItMatters: A refusal has to be a fact about the agent, not about us. Publishing "this endpoint did not answer" when the truth is "we asked too many things at once" is the same class of error as a topic filter that proves capability from a stranger's transaction: quiet, plausible, and wrong in the direction that makes our own page look decisive. It is also the reason the board's callable count is now consistent with the one payment this marketplace can prove it made.

findings.title: Rail 3 was enforcing its allowlist correctly on mainnet, and our own proof script could not tell.
findings.detail: prove-scope reported 6 proven, 0 failed, 4 inconclusive — and the four were the assertions that matter: in-scope allowed, out-of-scope refused, withheld selector refused, revoked call fails. Two defects in the script, neither in the rail. First, the in-scope baseline computed `signature.slice(0, indexOf("("))` — the function *name*, "mint", cast `as Hex` — then discarded that object and sent `data: "0x"`. The baseline exercised no selector at all, and every comparison was drawn against it. Second, the classifier read `shortMessage ?? details`, and Porto's shortMessage is the constant string "An error occurred while executing calls." for every outcome. The discriminating text was one field away, in `details`: `UnauthorizedCall(UnauthorizedCall { keyHash: 0xb4a3…, target: 0xfd36e2c2…, data: 0xb0772d0b })` — the Altana account naming the exact target and the exact four bytes it refused. With both fixed the same rail scores 8 proven and 0 failed against a session that existed for real.
findings.whyItMatters: The rail had been right the whole time. The account refuses an out-of-scope target and a withheld selector by name, an in-scope call fails at the target rather than at the policy, and revocation makes the key unknown to the relay. None of that changed today; only our ability to read it did. A proof that reads the first field that happens to be set will report a working system as unproven, and the same habit pointed the other way reports a broken one as fine — which is exactly what the predecessor project did when it matched a regex against the whole serialised error and called seven of eight assertions passed. The rule this leaves behind: search the field that discriminates, and if you cannot say which field that is, you do not yet have a proof.

findings.title: The Altana SDK ships a policy address the network does not use, and it makes every ERC-8183 escrow unfundable.
findings.detail: `@altananetwork/sdk@0.7.1` reports chain 97's dispute policy as 0x4F4678D4…78A6. That contract is deployed and answers disputeWindow() with 86,400. No job on the network is registered against it. Every live registerJob in the last four thousand blocks names 0xd6a42175…1cEA instead, whose window is 900 seconds — found by scanning the router's own logs for a call that succeeded and reading the address out of its calldata.
findings.whyItMatters: The failure is silent and total. registerJob reverts with an unnamed custom error, so the policy is never bound, so fund reverts with PolicyNotSet() and the escrow can never be filled. Nothing in either error says 'wrong policy'. Rail 2 was dead for this reason and nobody had noticed, because `npm run prove-hire` had been advertised in package.json for the life of the rail while pointing at a file that was never written. It also vindicates the plan's own figure and corrects a correction made earlier the same day: this repository briefly recorded testnet's dispute window as 24 hours and marked the plan's 900 seconds as wrong. The plan was right. The 24 hours belonged to a contract nobody uses. When a constant and the chain disagree, the chain is the constant.
findings.reproduce: npm run prove-hire, or read POLICY_OVERRIDE in packages/shared/src/addresses.ts

findings.title: ERC-8183's settlement policy is not pluggable by anyone. The router whitelists it, and says so by name.
findings.detail: A fresh job (1148) was created on chain 97 so that job state could not be a confound, then registerJob was simulated three times against the same job with only the policy address changed. The live policy 0xd6a42175…1cEA succeeded. The Altana SDK's own 0x4F4678D4…78A6 — a deployed policy contract of identical size that answers disputeWindow() correctly — reverted. An arbitrary deployed contract reverted identically. The revert is a custom error, 0xc94463e3, recovered by brute-forcing candidate signatures against keccak: **PolicyNotWhitelisted()**.
findings.whyItMatters: The plan's second discontinuity rests on one sentence: 'The policy is a pluggable contract bound per job via registerJob. That pluggability is the opening.' It is not open. The router accepts an allowlist that Altana controls, so an OutcomePolicy written here cannot be bound to a live job by us, today, at any price. This does not kill the idea — it relocates it. §6.4's fourth step, 'propose it upstream to Altana and BNB Chain as a reference implementation', stops being the last step and becomes the only path to step 2. The contract is still worth writing, as the artifact that makes the proposal concrete, and it must be described as a proposal rather than as a live settlement route. The general lesson is the one this repository keeps relearning: a capability described in documentation is a hypothesis until something calls it. Three of today's findings have this shape — a stale policy address, absent B402 usage fields, and now an allowlist nobody mentioned.
findings.reproduce: simulate registerJob(jobId, <any address>) on the router; only the whitelisted policy returns OK
